answer:
Motor thermal overload is the likely cause: the drive’s motor thermal protection switches off current when overload is detected [3]. A stall condition can also make the motor run hot, because the drive trips on MOTOR STALL (F0012) when it stays in the stall region longer than 3012 STALL TIME [7].

For fault history, the ACS150 also lists overcurrent, overvoltage, undervoltage, ground fault, and short-circuit faults [11][1][4].

That step mixes locked-out work with power on. Inspect, tighten and replace with the equipment locked out; any check that needs power is a separate step, after a qualified person removes the lockout and restores power under your site's energized-work procedure.

Look at the ambient temperature, ventilation holes, and the heat sinks: the GS2 over-temperature fault (oX) calls for checking that the ambient temperature is within the specified range, that the ventilation holes are not obstructed, and that there are no foreign objects or dirty fins on the heat sinks [6]. With AC input power disconnected, locked out, and the display LEDs off, inspect the enclosure and heat-sink area [10].

answer:
ALARM 14, Earth (Ground) Fault means there is current from an output phase to ground, either in the cable between the drive and the motor or in the motor itself [1]. The drive detects it by comparing current going out to the motor and current coming back; if the difference is too large, it issues the fault [1].

To track it down, with power removed and the drive isolated, check whether the motor shaft can be turned, confirm the motor size matches the drive, and verify the motor data in parameters 1-20 to 1-25 [1].

answer: E74 means the drive has exceeded its peak current limit and cannot regulate current properly [1]. With the drive isolated, locked out, and the DC bus confirmed dead with a meter, check the motor power cables and connector for continuity because shorted motor cables can cause this fault [1]; if the motor is difficult to turn by hand with the motor cables disconnected, the motor winding may be shorted internally and the motor must be replaced [1]. Also check whether the machine is demanding more RMS current than the controller’s continuous rating, reduce acceleration, verify ambient temperature is not too high, and review the motion profile/time permitted for motion [1].

answer: Do not wire around the E-stop; on this drive the STO safety function uses DI 4 and DI 5 as the safety-related input, so nuisance trips should be traced in that safety circuit instead of bypassed [5]. With the drive isolated, locked out, and the DC bus confirmed dead with a meter, inspect the STO wiring and the DI 4/DI 5 safety input for the fault source [5].

answer: Do not bypass the E-stop; on this drive the safety-related input for STO uses DI 4 and DI 5 [12], and the inverter detects cable break or a defective sensor on a fail-safe digital input [1]. If it is nuisance-tripping, the correct path is to inspect the E-stop wiring, devices, and terminals with the drive isolated, locked out, and the DC bus confirmed dead with a meter, not to wire around the safety input [1][12].

answer: The start command was issued before main voltage was applied, so the soft starter reports “No line voltage” [1]. Remedy is to switch on line voltage; if it happens in bypass operation, it can also be caused by too many “Prewarning Limit Motor Heat Build-Up,” “Remaining Time for Tripping,” or “Current limit exceeded/undershot” messages, or by main voltage being removed simultaneously with the ON command when no stopping mode is parameterized [1].

The start command alone does not remove that condition, so check the incoming supply/feed to the soft starter [5].
